Consider ABG, CXR, and blood glucose as initial tests if appropriate; rule out intrinsic lung disease, heart disease, and pulmonary embolism if clinically suspected. C
Screen for anxiety disorders using validated tools. B
Treatment should focus on correcting the underlying conditions. For psychogenic hyperventilation, treat panic or anxiety disorder using medical or cognitive therapy. B

background.definition: Hyperventilation is breathing in excess of the body's metabolic demand. It is a common problem among patients presenting to urgent care and emergency department settings. It is characterized by rapid or deep breathing, sometimes called overbreathing.

list.listitem: Prevalence: 9.5% among adults
Incidence: 0.9 cases per 100 patients per year.

ORGANIC: Pulmonary diseases such as asthma, pneumonia, COPD, interstitial lung disease and pulmonary embolism. Cardiac/GI diseases, eg, cardiac failure, pulmonary hypertension, liver failure. CNS, eg, central neurogenic hyperventilation, tumours of the midbrain, pons and medulla. Metabolic/ID: hypoxemia, acidemia, fever/sepsis. Acute pain syndromes.
PSYCHIATRIC: anxiety, panic attacks, factitious hyperventilation.
PHYSIOLOGIC: pregnancy, prolonged speech.
DRUGS: salicylate poisoning, beta adrenergic agonists, steroids, methylxantines.
Increased respiratory drive is mediated by the behavioral, metabolic or respiratory control systems.
The ensuing hypoxemia stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors and the afferent vagal receptors in the lungs, airways and the central nervous system.
This results in cough, bronchoconstriction and hyperventilation.
The magnitude of the response is attenuated by hypocapnia and subsequent increase in PH.
Alkalemia produces neurologic symptoms including syncope, dizziness and seizure activity due to cerebral vasoconstriction.
The resulting decreased free calcium may cause carpopedal spasm, tetany and paresthesia.
Prophylactic hyperventilation is not recommended for people with traumatic brain injury. B

Neurosurgical guidelines recommend hyperventilation as a temporizing measure to reduce raised intracranial pressure, but a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for hyperventilation for severe head injury. C
Suspect hyperventilation in patients presenting with rapid breathing, dyspnea, chest pain, paresthesias, and repeated sighing. C
Consider ABG, CXR, and blood glucose as initial tests if appropriate. C
Consider pulmonary embolism heart disease, and intrinsic lung disease; additional testing may be required to rule out these conditions. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Fever, obvious source of infection, hypothermia, tachycardia, leucocytosis, leukopenia
Decreased urinary output, azotemia, nausea. vomiting, anorexia, elevated creatinine
Diaphoresis, palpitations, tremulousness, tachycardia, irritability, and insomnia
Diarrhea, tachycardia, hypotension, decreased PH, decreased appetite, altered mental status
Abdominal pain, altered mental status, nausea, vomiting, tinnitus
Chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, palpitations, hypoxemia, cough, dyspnea

list.listitem: Patients may present with dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, palpitations. Initial evaluation should include screening for panic attack and generalized anxiety disorders.
Mildly elevated blood pressure is common.
Approximately 25% of patients report neurological symptoms ncluding dizziness, ataxia, tremor, hallucination, headaches, lightheadedness, and memory impairment.
Patients may appear to have "repeated sighing" and report paresthesias.
Gastrointestinal symptoms include epigastric pain, bloating, and vomiting.
If appropriate, consider blood glucose, ABG, and chest radiograph on initial testing.

ABG is the most useful initial diagnostic test, and in hyperventilation it is characterized by a decrease in pCO2. Increased pH indicates respiratory alkalosis, while decreased pH suggests metabolic acidosis. In primary alveolar hyperventilation, pH might not necessarily be alkalemic if mixed acid−base disorder is present.

Arterial pO2 is typically elevated. If hyperventilation is due to pulmonary causes, the arterial-alveolar pO2 difference is widened. In psychogenic hyperventilation, ABG abnormalities will not persist during sleep. HCO3 is decreased in chronic hyperventilation.
Chest radiograph should be considered for all patients with unexplained hyperventilation.
Consider pulmonary function tests and home peak flow measurements depending on the results of the initial evaluation.

If pulmonary embolism is a possible cause, evaluate the likelihood using validated clinical decision rule and consider further testing (d-dimer and/or high resolution chest CT or ventilation perfusion scan).
Consider ECG and/or echocardiogram to rule out pulmonary hypertension and orther cardiac etiologies.
Suspect hyperventilation in patients presenting with dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, palpitations, repeated sighing, or paresthesias.
Evaluate for panic disorder or generalized anxiety disorder using validated screening tool.
Consider elements of the differential diagnosis shown below.
Consider ABG and CXR on initial testing.
Depending on clinical presentation, consider further diagnostic testing for pulmonary embolism, coronary artery disease, or chronic lung disease.
Beta blockers may decrease the the sympathetic symptoms of hyperventilation. B
Antidepressants and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) may be effective in treating underlying panic or anxiety disorders among patients with hyperventilation syndrome. B
Breathing exercises have uncertain benefits for adults and children with hyperventilation syndrome. B
Treatment is directed at the underlying disorder.
Beta-blockers: They have been used to control the sympathetically mediated symptoms such as palpitation, tremors, sweating, and tachycardia. Excercise caution in asthmatics.

Antidepressants: Compared to placebo, antidepressants appear to be effective as monotherapy for panic disorder, based on low-quality evidence. Combined therapy using antidepressants and benzodiazepines has insufficient evidence for efficacy and safety in the treatment of panic disorder.

Tricyclic antidepressants: Clomipramine and imipramine have been found to normalize pCO2 in hyperventilation syndrome, but evidence regarding patient oriented outcomes and symptom improvement is lacking.
There is currently insufficient evidence to support the use of acupuncture in respiratory disorders such as hyperventilation.

Abdominal breathing using the diaphragm may lead to the subjective improvement in dyspnea associated with hyperventilation. Diaphragmatic breathing may also decrease the respiratory rate and provide the patient a sense of control.
CBT may be effective in treating anxiety disorders in children and adolescents. Consider referral for psychotherapy including stress management or behavioral therapy such as controlled breathing.

Consider physiotherapist referral for breathing exercises. However, two separate Cochrane reviews concluded that breathing exercises have uncertain benefits for adults and children with hyperventilation syndrome.

Inhalation of low concentration of CO2 has been found to provide relief in some patients whose alkalemia is causing cardiac arrythmias, parathesia, tetany and acute cerebral vasoconstriction. Long term reductions have been achieved in severe panic attacks and hyperventilation by using end-tidal CO2 breathing therapy.
Breathing into a paper bag is recommended in some patients but may be dangerous in those with significant cardiopulmonary disorders due to hypoxia.
Inpatient care is not usually necesasry except in circumstances when serious organic problems cannot be ruled out.
Many patients can be managed by their primary care physicians. Consultation with psychiatrist, psychologist or respiratory therapist with expertise in hyperventilation management may be considered.
